title: Week 6 Assessment: Leadership, Creativity and Knowledge
intro: This assessment checks how you lead, generate ideas, adapt and communicate what you know. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a leadership role-play and a written task. Think about what you would genuinely do.

items.prompt: You lead a three-person project. One member is repeatedly late with tasks, and the deadline is in five days. What is the best step?

options.text: Redo their work silently every time.
options.feedback: This hides the problem and burns you out.

options.text: Talk privately, ask what is blocking them, agree a specific plan with check-in times and adjust the load if needed.
options.feedback: It combines empathy, clarity and accountability.

options.text: Announce their failures to the whole group.
Ignore it until the deadline passes.

items.why: Good leaders address the issue early, privately and with a plan.

items.setup: Your team's client has just changed an important requirement, and a teammate is upset because their work may be wasted.

turns.they: This is so unfair. All my work is wasted!

options.text: That is just how it goes, deal with it.
options.reply: You do not care at all.

options.text: I understand why that is frustrating. Let us look at what can be reused and plan the changes together.
options.feedback: It validates feelings and moves to action.

options.text: Maybe we should blame the client.
options.feedback: Blame does not help the project.

turns.they: Some of it can be reused, but the deadline has not moved.

options.text: We will work through the night.
Let us list the changes, estimate each, agree what is essential and discuss moving one item with the client.
options.feedback: Impact assessment and options are the right response.

options.reply: The client will not like that.

turns.they: Who will talk to the client about the timeline?

options.text: I will, and I will send a written summary of the impact and options today.
options.feedback: Taking ownership and confirming in writing.

options.text: Wait and see what they say.
options.reply: We do not have much time.

items.why: Acknowledge feelings, assess impact, give options and take ownership of communication.

items.prompt: Your campus library has long queues at peak hours. Write 100 to 130 words: reframe the problem as two How Might We questions, list at least four varied ideas and state how you would test the best one cheaply.

descriptors.3: Cheap test with a clear measure.

items.modelAnswer: HMW 1: How might we make the first hour of the library peak less crowded? HMW 2: How might we let students borrow without queueing? Ideas: self-checkout kiosks, a mobile pre-booking list, a pickup shelf, staggered class-wise slots, a returns drop box. Cheap test: for one week, set up a pickup shelf for pre-booked books and measure average waiting time compared with the previous week using a simple tally sheet.
items.guidance: Strong answers reframe with open questions, offer varied ideas and propose a cheap test with a measurable result. Avoid proposing an expensive solution first.
